pr.title: MIR required_consts, mentioned_items: ensure we do not forget to fill these lists
pr.description: Bodies initially get created with empty required_consts and mentioned_items, but at some point those should be filled. Make sure we notice when that is forgotten.
pr.author: RalfJung

processing.reason: The PR is invariant-hardening for compiler metadata, not a demonstrated executable miscompile. `required_consts` and `mentioned_items` are compile-time MIR bookkeeping lists used for const-eval checks, promotion, monomorphization, and inlining; changing their representation from an always-empty `Vec` to `Option` makes omitted initialization panic rather than silently read as empty. There is no source-grounded runtime value transformation justified by the patch: omissions affect whether compiler checks or collection occur, not the value computed by a Rust function. Emulating the omission by returning an artificial list length or otherwise fabricating a numeric difference would test an unrelated rewrite, not the historical change. Therefore no valid original/transformed executable pair can be validated under the task constraints.

analysis.originalLogic: MIR `Body` construction initialized `required_consts` and `mentioned_items` to empty `Vec`s (`required_consts: Vec::new()`, `mentioned_items: Vec::new()`) in `Body::new`, `Body::new_cfg_only`, and custom MIR construction. Consumers iterated those vectors directly (`for &const_ in &body.required_consts`, `for item in &body.mentioned_items`). `RequiredConstsVisitor` collected into an external vector and the caller assigned it to the body; `MentionedItems` was registered inside the `run_passes` list and directly assigned `body.mentioned_items`; `PromoteTemps` pushed a promoted body's consts into `self.promoted.required_consts`; inlining extended the caller's lists directly from the callee.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: Allowing a MIR body to retain the default empty metadata lists as though they had been computed. In the historical code, "not yet filled" and "computed and genuinely empty" were indistinguishable, so a body that bypassed or skipped the relevant computation could still be read by const-eval, monomorphization, promotion, or inlining as if it had no required consts and no mentioned items. The patch changes the representation to `Option` and makes the omission observable by panicking on an unset read and by asserting lists are set only once. This is invariant-hardening: the supplied patch does not demonstrate a previously observed miscompile or wrong MIR output.
analysis.inputDomain: Rust source that produces MIR bodies beyond the ordinary optimized-MIR pass pipeline: async closures with by-move bodies, coroutines/generators, const-promotion candidates, generic functions whose MIR syntactically mentions unevaluated constants, ADT constructors, drop/call shims, custom MIR, and bodies with `injection_phase` set. Relevant configurations include optimization levels that enable inlining/promotion and paths that construct shims or ADT constructor bodies.
analysis.summary: Make `Body.required_consts` and `Body.mentioned_items` optional, set-once metadata so forgetting to compute them cannot silently masquerade as an empty computed list. `RequiredConstsVisitor` must be computed before promotion, `MentionedItems` must run even when `run_passes` would skip an injected body, and bodies that bypass the pass manager (shims, ADT constructors, by-move async closure bodies, promoted bodies) need explicit initialization. Inlining and promotion must consume the accessor rather than treating an unset list as empty.
analysis.trigger: A MIR body is created or reached outside the normal `run_passes` pipeline: `injection_phase` is set, the body is a by-move async closure body or promoted body, or it is a shim/ADT constructor. Also triggered when inlining or promotion reads/extends `required_consts` or `mentioned_items` before they have been computed.
preconditions: A `mir::Body` has been built and its `required_consts`/`mentioned_items` must be valid before const-eval, monomorphization, inlining, or promotion consumes them.
The body may not have gone through the ordinary optimized-MIR pass manager (shims, ADT constructors, by-move async closure bodies, custom MIR).
`run_passes` may skip a pass when `injection_phase` is set, so `MentionedItems` cannot rely on that pipeline for such bodies.
Promotion creates a new promoted body and must give that body its own computed `required_consts`; the surrounding body receives promoted consts separately.
pitfalls: Treating an empty `required_consts` or `mentioned_items` vector as proof that the body has none, when the list may simply never have been computed.
Registering `MentionedItems` only in the normal pass list: `run_passes` may skip it for injected bodies.
Forgetting the associated by-move async closure body, which is not itself run through the passes but is tagged along by the pass manager.
Letting a promoted MIR body share or inherit the source body's required-const list instead of assembling and setting its own.
Reading or extending caller/callee lists during inlining without ensuring the caller and callee lists have been computed.
Assuming shims and ADT constructors need metadata computed by the ordinary passes; they need explicitly set empty/suitable lists because they bypass those passes.
analysis.testStrategy: Use debug-assertion-enabled compiler tests/UI tests exercising: async closures whose by-move body is tagged along, coroutine/generator bodies, const promotion candidates, generic functions mentioning constants, inlining across such bodies, ADT constructors, and shims. Verify that reading `required_consts()`/`mentioned_items()` panics when a body never computed them, and that setting a list twice asserts. Compare MIR/const-eval/monomorphization behavior for otherwise identical programs with and without promotion or a by-move async closure. The supplied patch contains no regression test changes, so these are focused strategies rather than observed test results; no compiler was built and no execution is claimed.
